title: The Golden Apple and the Trojan War

blocks.text: Once there was a great wedding. A hero named Peleus was marrying Thetis, a sea goddess, and all the gods and goddesses were invited. All except one. Nobody invited Eris, the goddess of arguments, because wherever she went, people started quarreling.
Eris was furious. She crept up to the wedding feast and rolled a golden apple onto the table. On it were written three words: "For the most beautiful."
Three goddesses reached for it at once. "It's mine," said Hera, the queen of the gods. "No, it's mine," said Aphrodite, the goddess of love. "It's obviously mine," said Athena, the goddess of wisdom.
They asked Zeus to choose. But Zeus was too clever to get mixed up in that. "Ask the young shepherd Paris, on Mount Ida," he said. "He'll decide."
So the three goddesses went to find Paris, who was really a prince of the city of Troy. Each goddess tried to win him over with a present.
"Choose me," said Hera, "and I will make you a great and powerful king."
"Choose me," said Athena, "and I will make you wise, and famous in war."
"Choose me," said Aphrodite, "and I will give you the most beautiful woman in the world to be your wife."
Paris gave the apple to Aphrodite.

The most beautiful woman in the world was named Helen. But she was already married, to Menelaus, the king of Sparta in Greece. Paris visited Sparta, and when he sailed home to Troy, Helen went with him.
Menelaus was furious. Long ago, all the kings of Greece had promised to help whoever married Helen if anyone ever took her away. So Menelaus called on them to keep their promise.

One king, Odysseus, did not want to go. He loved his wife, Penelope, and his baby son, Telemachus. So he pretended to have gone crazy. He tied a donkey and an ox to a plow, and walked up and down his field sowing salt instead of seeds. But a clever messenger laid baby Telemachus right in front of the plow. Odysseus turned the plow aside so it would not hurt his son. Then everyone knew he was not crazy at all, and he had to go.
A thousand ships sailed for Troy, full of the greatest heroes of Greece. The bravest of all was Achilles, the son of Thetis. On the side of Troy, the bravest was Prince Hector, Paris's older brother.

Troy had tall, strong walls. The Greeks camped outside them and fought, year after year. The gods took sides too. Hera and Athena helped the Greeks, because they were still angry with Paris. Aphrodite helped the Trojans. For nine long years, neither side could win.

Then, in the tenth year, Achilles had a terrible argument with Agamemnon, the leader of the Greeks. Agamemnon took away a prize that Achilles had won. Achilles was so angry that he went to his tent and refused to fight anymore.
Without Achilles, the Greeks began to lose. The Trojans pushed them all the way back to their ships, and set one of the ships on fire.
Achilles's best friend was named Patroclus. "Please," Patroclus begged, "if you won't fight, at least let me borrow your armor. When the Trojans see it, they'll think you've come back."
Achilles agreed. Patroclus put on Achilles's shining armor and charged into battle, and the Trojans ran away in fright. But then Hector came to meet him. They fought, and Patroclus was killed.

When Achilles heard, he cried out with grief so loud that his mother heard him from the bottom of the sea. Now he wished he had never left the battle. His mother asked Hephaestus, the blacksmith god, to make him new armor, the finest ever made. Achilles put it on and went back to the fight, angrier than anyone had ever seen him.

The Trojans fled back inside their walls. Only Hector stayed outside to face Achilles. His old father, King Priam, begged him to come in. But Hector would not hide. The two great heroes fought, and Achilles won. Hector fell.
King Priam's heart was broken. He wanted to give his son a proper funeral, but Achilles had taken Hector's body away.
So one night, the old king did something very brave. All alone, he went to Achilles's tent, in the middle of the Greek camp. He knelt in front of the man who had killed his son.
"Think of your own father," said Priam. "He is old like me, far away, and he misses you. I have lost so many sons. Please, give me back my Hector."

Achilles thought of his own father, and he began to cry. Priam cried too. For a long while, the two enemies sat and wept together. Then Achilles gently gave Hector back to his father, and promised that the Greeks would not fight while Troy held Hector's funeral.
The people of Troy mourned Hector for nine days. He was the bravest of them all.
But the war was not over yet. The story of how Troy fell at last is called "The Wooden Horse."

A simplified retelling of Thomas Bulfinch's “The Trojan War” in The Age of Fable (1855). The original is listed under Other versions. Bulfinch uses the Roman names Juno for Hera, Venus for Aphrodite, Minerva for Athena, Jupiter for Zeus and Vulcan for Hephaestus, and calls Odysseus Ulysses.
